explanation: Fires most strongly on the dot (or digit) inside software version numbers and product/year identifiers in technical text (e.g. '25.4[.]0', 'jquery/2.2[.]2', 'SQL Server 20[1]4', 'Runtime Version:4[.]0'); also scattered hits on code punctuation and some non-English subword tokens. Prose tokens give weak, unpredictable activation.

Fires in first-person/reader-experience framing of initial impressions or reactions, on tokens like 'first', 'struck', 'was', 'be', 'at', 'instantly' in phrases such as 'At first I thought', 'It struck me', 'When I first heard... I was', 'Don't be fooled', 'may seem', 'can't help but'. Strongest when the context describes how something seems or is perceived on first encounter.

Fires on the first subword fragment of a rare, often foreign or proper-noun word that is split into multiple tokens (e.g. 'R[akh]is', 'musik[sty]kker', 'Hizbul [Muj]ahideen', 'Talmud [Y]erushalmi', '[DIS]CLAIMED'), i.e. the start of an unfamiliar multi-token word. Common whole words fire weakly.

Fires on function/method tokens or operators in code that introduce a call taking arguments (e.g. 'Object.prototype.toString[.call](', '[len](', 'std::[move](', 'make[_pair](', 'strncmp', '==='), and on relational prepositions in prose that link a head noun to its argument ('function [of]', 'made [by]', 'relationship [between]', 'impact [on]'). Common theme: a token that opens an argument slot to be filled next.

Fires on an inner or initial subword piece of a long, uncommon word split into several tokens, especially technical, scientific, foreign or proper-name words (e.g. 'dend[rim]ers', 'Ad[ir]ondack', 'alk[oh]olikere', 'Quercus [rob]ur', 'd[iph]theria', 'pr[eds]edo'). Ordinary whole words and numbers fire weakly.

Fires in scientific/medical abstract text on words specifying the population or regime being studied, especially age groups ('pediatric', 'adults', 'infants', 'children', 'aged [ ]13', '68-year old') and physics regimes ('ultrac[old]', 'high [energy]'); top example is 'accelerate' ions. Mostly a 'study population/condition qualifier' detector in academic writing.

Fires on content words (often the second word of a technical compound or a descriptive term) in descriptive/technical prose: 'Disney [animated]', 'leaves are [alternate]', 'tandem [mass] spectrometry', 'coupled [plasma]', 'DC [motors]', 'hurricanes', plus odd code tokens like 'echo' and '.io'. No single clear shared feature beyond technical-noun-phrase completion.

Fires in contexts of reasoning, hypothesizing or asking for confirmation/solution: tokens like 'reasonable?' in 'Does that sound reasonable', 'hypo[thesize]', 'hypothesis', 'explain', 'missing [something]', 'Can't [be] hard', 'Am I [likely]', and math-problem tokens ('o'th [term]', 'for [p]'). Strongest on the word completing a question or hypothesis about what is true.

Fires on tokens inside quoted string literals in code (Python, JS, PHP, CSS-in-JS, config), e.g. '__[main]__', '[email]', '<[span]', 'h[1]', '[keywords]', especially the first token right after an opening quote. Prose quotes fire weakly.

Mixture: fires on the 'k'-containing subword in transliterated foreign names (Hok, Kok, Sok, Gok, Kank, Hock, k-oh-lrabi), on French/German 'plus'/'aber', on some digits in years/numbers, and on code tokens (indentation, 'Format', '("'). The Japanese/Turkish-style '-ok-' syllable names are the most consistent strand.

Fires on tokens in formal mathematical/statistical text marking parameters or conditions (variables like 'Z', 'N', 'alpha', 'sigma', 'sample [size]', 'under ... [the]') and on C++/Swift template brackets and template parameter separators ('template[<]', 'typename T[>]', 'TKey[,]'). Both are 'generic parameter' contexts.

Fires on indentation/whitespace and line-starting tokens in config or markup code (Apache RewriteCond/RewriteRule lines, XML '<' after indentation, Scheme '('), plus a scattering of prose function words ('a', 'the', ',' in lists, 'and'). The htaccess/config indentation strand is clearest; the prose hits are unpredictable.

Fires on diverse tokens with no evident shared feature: legal citation pieces ('No[.]', 'S.W.3[d]', 'CR[-]770', '(Ch)'), timestamps, '©', and assorted prose words ('so', 'all', 'large', 'unknown', 'for'). Legal docket/citation formatting is a partial theme.

Mixture: fires on forms of 'accelerate' ('accelerating', 'accelerated', 'accelerate'), on 'estate' in 'real estate', on '#define [pb]' in C macros, and on assorted subword/function tokens in various languages. The 'accelerate' strand is the most consistent.
